questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches, discuss in detail each of the following renewable energy technologies and identify how each contributes to making a home more eco-friendly: • evacuated tubes • wind turbines • photovoltaic panels.

rows.contextNote: 2. Wind turbine

options: Wind activates the turning of the blades and rotor. They spin the main shaft and gearbox, which spins the generator resulting in electrical output
They can be connected to batteries or the national grid

When the wind flows across the blade, the air pressure on one side of the blade decreases. The difference in air pressure across the two sides of the blade creates both lift and drag. The force of the lift is stronger than the drag and this causes the rotor to spin
An inverter is needed to convert the direct current (DC) voltage from the turbine to match the alternating current (AC) voltage required for domestic use
The control box is used to protect the invertor and turbine in strong winds. If the wind becomes too strong the control box will slow the turbine down
If the turbine sits on a tower, then a concrete foundation is generally required
Planning permission may however be required if it is thought that the turbine would interfere with the character of the landscape or a special amenity

rows.contextNote: 3. Photovoltaic cells

options: A photovoltaic panel is a collection of photovoltaic (PV) cells. Multiple panels can be wired together to form an array. In general, the larger the area of a module or array, the more electricity that will be produced

The solar panel system uses particles of light from the sun (photons) to separate electrons from atoms. The process of separating electrons causes the electrons to hit off metal conductor strips on the outside of the PV cells thus generating electricity
Excess electricity can be stored in batteries or sent back to the grid

No waste product is generated

questionText: Explain, with the aid of notes and freehand sketches, any five of the following: strip foundation; fascia board; airtight tape; wind turbine; septic tank; dovetail joint; wall tie; cordless jigsaw; underfloor heating.

rows.contextNote: Explain any five of the nine terms. Each term is marked separately: primary communication of relevant information 6 and other communication 4, in notes or sketches (the scheme reserves no fixed split between them). Strip foundation: a simple, common foundation for homes; concrete reinforced with steel for tensile strength; the wall placed centrally with loads spread at 45° to the ground; used where the soil has a good bearing capacity. Fascia board: gives a finished appearance and protects the house from the weather; part of the eaves with the soffit; carries the gutters; usually wood, PVC or aluminium. Airtight tape: a highly adhesive tape used with an airtight membrane at every junction of building elements and around door and window frames, preventing draughts and heat loss. Wind turbine: converts wind energy into mechanical energy that generates electricity; sustainable, reducing reliance on fossil fuels; commercial wind farms or smaller domestic turbines; horizontal- or vertical-axis. Septic tank: an underground chamber that collects, stores and treats domestic wastewater; anaerobic bacteria break down solids, which settle as sludge; treated water returns to the ground through the percolation area. Dovetail joint: a common joint in drawer and box construction and quality furniture; the slope of the tail (1:8 hardwood, 1:6 softwood) gives its tensile strength; cut by hand or with a router jig. Wall tie: ties the two leaves of a cavity wall into one stable unit, embedded in the mortar; stainless steel or basalt fibre (less thermal bridging); lengths to suit the cavity. Cordless jigsaw: cuts shapes and curves with a reciprocating blade; battery powered, portable and safer without a lead; the base rests on the work and is pushed along; used on a range of materials. Underfloor heating: polyethylene pipes beneath the floor carry water heated by a heat pump; the floor becomes a large heat source with no cold spots and a constant temperature, replacing radiators; efficient at low temperatures.

options: Strip foundation
Fascia board
Airtight tape

stem: An extension to a house has a highly insulated flat roof with a waterproof roof covering, as shown.
questionText: Using the U-value of the roof obtained at 5(a) above and the following data, calculate the cost of heat lost annually through this roof: dimensions of flat roof 8.5 metres × 4.5 metres; average internal temperature 18 °C; average external temperature 5 °C; heating period 8 hours daily for 36 weeks per annum; cost of oil €1.25 per litre; calorific value of oil 37350 kJ per litre; 1000 watts: 1 kJ per second.

rows.contextNote: Heat loss = U-value × area × temperature difference = 0.104 × 38.25 × (18 − 5) = 51.714 watts (joules per second).

rows.verbatim: Heating duration - calculation for one year
rows.contextNote: Heating period = 60 × 60 × 7 × 8 × 36 = 7,257,600 seconds (2,016 hours).

rows.verbatim: Litres of oil - calculation for one year
rows.contextNote: Oil = 375,319 ÷ 37,350 = 10.04 litres per year.

rows.verbatim: Annual cost – calculation of heat loss PA
rows.contextNote: Annual cost = 10.04 × €1.25 = €12.53. The scheme’s alternative one-line method gives the same €12.53.

stem: The entry of light into rooms is a key consideration when designing a home.
questionText: The sketch shows a living room which measures 4.5 metres long by 4.2 metres wide. The living room has a vertical window and unobstructed views. An average illumination of 500 lux of daylight is required on the work plane. Calculate using the degree of efficiency method, or any other suitable method, the appropriate area of glazing required to provide the stated illumination. Assuming the illumination of a standard overcast sky to be 5000 lux.

rows.contextNote: Li = Lo × WF × E × window area ÷ floor area, where Li is the lux required, Lo the standard overcast sky (5000 lux), WF the window factor (0.5 for a vertical window) and E the efficiency coefficient (0.4).
Floor area = 4.5 × 4.2 = 18.9 m².

rows.verbatim: Using formula Li = Lo × WF × E

rows.contextNote: Two solving lines and the answer, 4 each: 500 × 18.9 = 1,000 W, so 9450 = 1,000 W; W = 9450 ÷ 1000; window area = 9.45 m².

questionText: Explain, with the aid of notes and freehand sketches, any five of the following: concrete mixer; smart radiator valve; ridge tile; triple glazing; balusters; cedar cladding; bridle joint; wood pellet stove; floor screed.

rows.contextNote: Explain any five of the nine terms. Each term is marked separately: primary communication of relevant information 6 and other communication 4, in notes or sketches (the scheme reserves no fixed split between them). Concrete mixer: a rotating drum that turns raw materials into concrete without segregation; small on-site batch mixers (electric, petrol or diesel) are hand loaded and make up to 200 litres per batch, so quality control is difficult; larger quantities come from a mixing plant in a ready-mix truck of 4–6 cubic metres, better regulated and poured directly into the work area. Smart radiator valve: fitted to new or existing radiators; integrated sensors measure the room temperature and signal to reduce or increase the flow of hot water; controlled from smart devices when the owners are away; each room can have its own temperature; reduces energy cost and use. Ridge tile: sits on the apex of the roof and seals the intersection of the two roof planes; traditionally bedded in mortar, now often fixed with integrated dry-fix systems; made from materials like the roof covering, in a variety of colours and profiles. Triple glazing: three panes of glass with cavities usually filled with an inert gas (argon, xenon or krypton); reduces noise and insulates better than double glazing; heavier and thicker, so it may not suit all frames; it can reduce solar gain, so some owners avoid it on the southern elevation. Balusters: vertical members between the handrail and string of a stairs, also called spindles; moulded, square or lathe-turned; must not let a 100 mm diameter sphere pass between them; made of wood, iron or plastic. Cedar cladding: naturally durable, lasting over 60 years without preservative treatment, which is only needed to avoid the weathered silver-grey colour; fixed horizontally or vertically to battens with stainless steel or galvanised fixings, as cedar reacts with ferrous metals; low embodied energy. Bridle joint: a common, strong woodworking joint with a large gluing area; a tee or corner bridle, removing one third of the material from one piece and two thirds from the other; used in frame construction and to join table rails to uprights. Wood pellet stove: heats a home by burning renewable pellets of compressed sawdust and waste wood; an auger feeds fuel steadily from a hopper for a constant flame needing little adjustment; a low-cost heating alternative with very low emissions and a smaller environmental impact. Floor screed: the final layer of the floor on which a floor finish is laid; traditionally sand and cement at 3:1 to 5:1, levelled with a tamping board; modern free-flowing calcium sulphate screeds self-level and suit underfloor heating, at 50–75 mm over pipes clipped to the rigid insulation.

stem: The sketch shows a bungalow which has been retrofitted. The owners have engaged skilled labour in the upgrade of their bungalow to meet the EnerPHit Passive House design standard.
questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches, discuss the importance of any two of the following when carrying out a retrofit to achieve the EnerPHit Passive House design standard: airtightness; windows; building fabric.

rows.verbatim: Discuss the importance of any two in EnerPHit design standard
rows.contextNote: Any two of the three, each notes 6 and sketches 6 = 12. EnerPHit is reached through the five Passive House principles (insulation, limited thermal bridging, triple glazing, airtightness, MVHR), modelled in the PHPP design tool; its space heating demand limit is 25 kWh/m² per year (Passive House 15). Airtightness: Air leakage prevented with airtightness membranes, airtight boards and tapes in timber frame and roofs, and a sand-cement scratch coat, plaster and airtightness paint in block walls; checks for leakage at each stage and a full airtightness test at the end; the EnerPHit target is under 1.0 air changes per hour at 50 Pascals (Passive House 0.6); without airtightness the insulation cannot perform. Windows: Passive House triple-glazed windows of 0.80 W/m²K or less (EnerPHit, installed, 0.85 W/m²K or less); frames in line with the external insulation to avoid a thermal bridge; shading and ventilation planned against summer overheating. Building fabric: Insulation increased to roof, floor and walls (U-value 0.120 W/m²K or less for EnerPHit) by cavity, external or internal insulation; quality workmanship to avoid thermal bridges; external insulation continued below ground level; airtightness and insulation achieved together.

options: Airtightness

Building fabric

questionText: Explain, with the aid of notes and freehand sketches, any five of the following: site planning notice; halving joint; faceplate turning; smart lighting; cordless drill; plywood; gulley trap; cavity closer; heat pump.

rows.contextNote: Explain any five of the nine terms. Each term is marked separately: primary communication of relevant information 6 and other communication 4, in notes or sketches (the scheme reserves no fixed split between them). Site planning notice: a public notice the applicant erects at the site when applying for planning permission, clearly visible and legible from the road, giving the applicant’s name, site address, type of application and nature of the development; required by planning regulations so the public can make observations or objections; in place for the first five weeks after lodgement, or the application may be invalid. Halving joint: a common, strong woodworking joint with a medium gluing area, made by removing half the material from each piece at the joint; cross, corner, T- or dovetail halving; used in framing and furniture. Faceplate turning: a woodturning method for large, flat circular items such as bowls and plates; the work piece is mounted on a faceplate on the headstock of the lathe; the tool rest supports the chisel; start slowly until the piece is balanced, then increase the speed. Smart lighting: lighting controlled remotely, often automatically, through a smartphone, tablet or voice commands over the internet; scheduling and timers; customised colour, brightness and ambiance; contributes to energy savings. Cordless drill: a portable power tool for drilling holes and driving screws, powered by rechargeable (usually lithium-ion) batteries; more convenient and versatile than a corded drill and usable where there is no power source; features such as an LED light and battery indicator. Plywood: an engineered panel of thin wood veneers glued with the grain of each layer perpendicular to the next for strength; used in construction, furniture and cabinet-making; a strong, relatively low-cost alternative to solid wood; marine plywood for high-moisture use. Gulley trap: a fitting in foul and rainwater drainage with a U-bend that holds water as a seal against sewer gases and odours entering the building; typically underground; needs regular maintenance. Cavity closer: closes the gap between the leaves of a cavity wall at wallplate level and around window and door openings; prevents thermal bridging, damp penetration, air infiltration and condensation; insulating foam or rigid board, 100–150 mm wide to suit the cavity. Heat pump: a device transferring heat from the air, water or ground into the home, distributed by underfloor heating or radiators; runs on electricity with a coefficient of performance of about 3–4; grants encourage the change from fossil-fuel heating.

options: Site planning notice
Halving joint
Faceplate turning
Smart lighting
Cordless drill
Plywood
Gulley trap
Cavity closer
Heat pump

questionText: Discuss in detail the importance of any two of the following in maintaining a positive health and safety culture among workers on a construction site: safety training; health and safety officer; risk assessment audit.

rows.verbatim: The importance of any two in maintaining a positive health and safety culture
rows.contextNote: Any two of the three, 6 each, discussing why each matters to a positive health and safety culture. Safety training: Safe Pass is mandatory and kept current through refresher courses; training builds awareness of site risks and the skills to identify them and follow best practice; specialist tickets for machinery and vehicles; monitoring and enforcing safe work practices; it may be a condition of the insurance provider. Health and safety officer: provides induction and ongoing training (working at heights, machinery use); develops emergency response plans; keeps first aid and emergency equipment available; ensures the correct PPE is worn; carries out safety inspections and risk assessments; reviews the safety statement; investigates, records and reports accidents. Risk assessment audit: provides a safe working environment; evaluates compliance with safety regulations and policies; identifies hazards and puts control measures in place where a risk cannot be eliminated (for fire: alarms, evacuation signage, drills, extinguishers); recommends improvements; identifies training needs; reduces accidents and liability.

options: Safety training
Health and safety officer

stem: The sketch shows the proposed design of a Passive House which is to be constructed in a rural setting.
questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches, discuss the importance of any two of the following in Passive House design: building form; foundation design; space heating energy demand.

rows.verbatim: Discuss the importance of any two in Passive House design
rows.contextNote: Any two of the three, each notes 5 and sketches 5 = 10. Building form: a compact, simple rectangular form with the smallest surface area (A/V ratio 0.7 or less) to cut heat loss, materials and cost; a narrow plan, one room deep, to maximise solar gain; clean lines in walls and roof that make airtightness easy. Foundation design: insulated ring-beam or passive raft foundations wrapped in insulation to eliminate thermal bridging; thermal blocks in the inner-leaf rising wall; 50–100 mm edge insulation at the floor/wall junction; thermally broken wall ties; a U-value of 0.10–0.15 W/m²K. Space heating energy demand: passive house space-heating demand of no more than 15 kWh/m² per year; quality workmanship in airtightness and insulation; eliminating thermal bridges; solar gain through well-designed fenestration; solar shading, thermal mass and controlled ventilation to keep about 20 °C all year.

Foundation design
Space heating energy demand

stem: The external wall of a house built in the 1970s is of single leaf hollow-block construction with an external render. Insulated plasterboard is fixed to the internal surface of the wall. It is proposed to upgrade the thermal properties of the external wall by installing external insulation as shown.
questionText: It has been decided that the wall at 5(a) above should meet the Passive House standard, by further increasing the thickness of the external insulation. Calculate the thickness of additional external insulation required to achieve a U-value of 0.11 W/m2 ºC.

rows.verbatim: Resistance for U-value for 0.11 W/m2 °C (using R=1/U)
rows.contextNote: Required resistance = 1 ÷ 0.11 = 9.091 m²K/W (the scheme first finds R = 1 ÷ 0.221 = 4.525 for the wall at 5(a)).
Additional resistance = 9.091 − 4.525 = 4.566 m²K/W.
R = T ÷ k for the external insulation: 4.566 = T ÷ 0.030.
T = 4.566 × 0.030 = 0.137 m, so 137 mm of additional insulation. Alternative calculation methods are acceptable.

sourceMaterial.presentationNote: All printed data are retained in the original question. Parts (b) and (c) use the U-value from part (a); the scheme’s worked answers are U = 0.221 W/m²°C, an annual cost of €76.34 and 137 mm of additional insulation.

stem: The drawing shows the ground floor plan of a two-storey semi-detached house and a portion of the rear garden. The external walls of the house are 400 mm concrete block walls with a full-fill insulated cavity. The rear wall M-M is south facing. The owners need an additional space for use as a study and occasionally as a family space. The space is to have internal dimensions of 5.0 metres × 3.0 metres as shown. The following options are being considered: (i) building a single-storey extension onto the rear of the house at A. or (ii) building a detached, free-standing space in the garden at B.
questionText: Discuss in detail two advantages and two disadvantages of each option listed at (i) and (ii) above. — Option A

rows.contextNote: An advantage of the single-storey extension at A, discussed for this house (3). Such as: saves on construction and insulation costs; conserves space in the rear garden; more efficient energy use, as it minimises the area of external walling; more freedom in using and dividing the total living space.

A second, different advantage of the extension at A (3). Such as: easy, economical connection to existing services (space heating, plumbing, ventilation, electrical distribution); a compact plan that supports regular social interaction across the generations of the family.

A disadvantage of the extension at A (3). Such as: disturbs the well-proportioned original layout; creates a large undifferentiated space that needs careful design; can reduce the natural lighting and ventilation of the kitchen/dining room; more energy for lighting and heating a large space.

A second, different disadvantage of the extension at A (3). Such as: fewer discrete rooms for a quieter environment; may spoil the view from the existing kitchen and dining area; continuity of insulation and weatherproofing at the roof and wall abutment; spanning the larger opening in the existing external wall may need strengthening and RSJs; misses the chance to connect the garden with the living spaces.

questionText: Discuss in detail two advantages and two disadvantages of each option listed at (i) and (ii) above. — Option B

rows.contextNote: An advantage of the detached, free-standing space at B, discussed for this house (3). Such as: keeps the existing relationship between the kitchen/dining area and the outside; minimises disruption during construction; maintains natural lighting to the existing rooms; greater privacy in a distinct room in the garden.

A second, different advantage of the space at B (3). Such as: space for a young or older family member; more freedom of design and more natural lighting in the new building; a closer link between room and garden; isolation for activities that need quiet or are noisy; does not overshadow the existing kitchen and dining room.

A disadvantage of the space at B (3). Such as: a larger external envelope with higher insulation costs; the inconvenience of crossing the garden to reach it; possibly higher heating costs from an extra external door and reduced airtightness.

A second, different disadvantage of the space at B (3). Such as: garden space lost to paths; unusable spaces near the external doors; fragmentation of family living space; the cost of access for all and of connecting services (heating, plumbing and waste, electrical). The scheme prints this list under the heading 3(b)(ii); it belongs to part (a), option B.

questionText:
Using the following data, calculate the U-value of the external wall of a new dwelling house. The wall is of concrete block construction, with a 250 mm cavity. The cavity is a full-fill insulated cavity, with polystyrene bead insulation as shown.
Specification of external wall: external render thickness 16 mm; concrete block outer leaf thickness 100 mm; cavity width 250 mm; concrete block inner leaf thickness 100 mm; internal plaster thickness 12 mm.
Thermal data of external wall: resistance of external surface (R) 0.048 m² °C/W; conductivity of external render (k) 0.720 W/m °C; conductivity of concrete blocks (k) 1.440 W/m °C; conductivity of polystyrene bead (k) 0.031 W/m °C; conductivity of internal plaster (k) 0.220 W/m °C; resistance of internal surface (R) 0.122 m² °C/W.

rows.contextNote: Use a clear resistance table or equivalent method. Convert layer thicknesses from mm to m; R = thickness/conductivity, add both surface resistances and all five material layers, then U = 1/Rtotal. The rubric heading “Insulated concrete ground floor” is a source error: the paper and the worked solution describe the specified external wall.

Seven resistances, 3 each: the five material layers by R = thickness/conductivity, with thicknesses converted from mm to m, and the two given surface resistances. External surface Rse = 0.048 (given; do not divide it by a thickness); external render 0.016/0.720 = 0.02222222; outer concrete-block leaf 0.100/1.440 = 0.06944444; polystyrene bead 0.250/0.031 = 8.06451613 (the cavity is fully filled, so no separate air-cavity resistance); inner concrete-block leaf 0.100/1.440 = 0.06944444 (both leaves count); internal plaster 0.012/0.220 = 0.05454545; internal surface Rsi = 0.122 (given). All in m²·°C/W.

U = 1/Rtotal = 1/8.45017269 = 0.11834078 W/(m²·°C), approximately 0.1183 W/(m²·°C). The rubric awards 1 mark for the formula alone within this 3-mark criterion, not an additional mark. The remaining criteria stay at their own published 3-mark allocations.

questionText:
Using the U-value obtained at 5(a) and the data given below, calculate the cost of heat lost annually through the external walls of the new house - as specified at 5(a) above.
Data for both houses: area of external wall of each house 150 m²; average internal temperature 20 °C; average external temperature 6 °C; heating period 8 hours per day, every day for 35 weeks per annum; cost of oil 95 cent per litre; calorific value of oil 37350 kJ per litre; 1000 watts: 1kJ per second.

rows.contextNote: Use heat-loss rate = U × A × ΔT, with ΔT = 20 − 6 = 14 °C. For this house, 0.11834078 × 150 × 14 ≈ 248.51563 W (J/s). Use the U-value appropriate to this house; rate alone is not annual energy or cost.

8 × 7 × 35 = 1,960 hours = 7,056,000 seconds. The worked scheme prints “3,157 hours” beside the correct seconds; that parenthetical hours figure is an error. Follow the paper’s schedule and the correct seconds, not 3,157 hours.
Annual wall heat loss = heat-loss rate × 7,056,000 / 1,000 ≈ 1,753,526.29 kJ. The factor 1,000 converts J to kJ; keep watts, seconds and the oil calorific value in consistent units.

rows.verbatim: Litres of oil for one year
rows.contextNote: Litres = annual energy / 37,350 ≈ 46.94850 litres. This uses the calorific value given in the paper; do not invent an unstated boiler-efficiency factor.

Cost = litres × €0.95 ≈ €44.60107. Using unrounded values gives €44.60 to the nearest cent. The scheme also prints €44.58 using a rounded U = 0.1183 and intermediate truncation; calculating directly with that U gives €44.58570 (normally €44.59). Accept coherent rounding consistent with the working rather than demanding the source’s truncation. Alternative direct or proportional methods may earn the equivalent published criteria; do not award the same calculation twice.

stem: The roof of a new house, as shown, is a traditional cut roof and has a pitch of 45 degrees. The house has an internal width of 6.0 metres and the roof is highly insulated. The drawing shows an outline section through a two-storey house having a 450 mm external concrete block wall with a 250 mm full-fill insulated cavity. questionText: Discuss the importance of designing a building envelope that is thermal bridge free.

rows.verbatim: Discussion (point 1) - 2 marks for point, 4 marks for discussion
rows.contextNote: Give a distinct valid point (2) and develop its importance (4). Source-supported routes include reduced heat loss and heating demand; more even internal surface temperatures and comfort; less risk of cold surfaces reaching dew point, condensation and mould; less material deterioration and associated health effects. Explain the causal relationship, not just a label, and avoid repeating the other point. Thermal bridging is local increased conduction; airtightness alone does not remove every conductive bridge.

stem: Light is what architecture is all about. It is as fundamental for the soul as air, fire, earth and water. Light has been one of the key elements of architecture since the Modern movement began (and glass technology improved) at the turn of the 20th century. Yet, light has traditionally been lacking in Irish homes. Many old cottages only have windows on the south side and none on the north. Now glass has improved and windows can be made with incredibly low U-values (meaning it doesn’t let the cold through), so you can now have large glazed areas without heat loss. We need light and instinctively search for it. People move to the part of the room where there is natural light and children instinctively play in pools of light. Adapted from LOVE YOUR HOME Secrets to a Successful Space by Dermot Bannon (2014) Published by Gill & Macmillan. ISBN: 978 07171 6448 6

questionRef: 2015 OL Q2(a) — filling the cavity with insulation
stem: The sketch shows a dwelling house which was built over 40 years ago. The external wall is a 300 mm concrete block wall with a 100 mm cavity. There is no insulation in the cavity. It is proposed to insulate the external wall by: filling the cavity with insulation and adding an external system of insulation to the wall.
questionText: It is proposed to insulate the external wall by: filling the cavity with insulation. Using notes and freehand sketches, show the steps to be followed in applying each system of insulation to the wall.

rows.verbatim: Filling the cavity with insulation – Notes
rows.contextNote: Three valid steps, 4 marks each. Typical procedure (carried out by specialist firms): 22 mm diameter holes are drilled through the external leaf, usually spaced about 800 mm horizontally and 1350 mm vertically; special care is taken at damp proof courses and at heads of windows and doors, with extra holes drilled around openings so the cavity fills properly; polystyrene beads are pumped into the cavity while a light coating of glue is applied, setting into a solid structure; when pumping is complete the holes are filled. Other valid steps are acceptable.

rows.verbatim: Filling the cavity with insulation – Sketches
rows.contextNote: Quality of sketches for the cavity-fill steps: excellent 8, good 6, fair 4. The scheme sketches show the drill entering the outer leaf and the hole spacing on the wall.

questionText: It is proposed to insulate the external wall by: adding an external system of insulation to the wall. Using notes and freehand sketches, show the steps to be followed in applying each system of insulation to the wall.

rows.verbatim: Adding an external system of insulation to the wall – Notes
rows.contextNote: Three valid steps, 4 marks each. Typical procedure: the first row of insulation boards is fixed in place resting on a stainless steel track; boards are fixed in position with a special adhesive, and all rows are fixed and the adhesive allowed to set; mechanical fixings (typically about seven per square metre, longer for thicker boards) are installed by drilling through the insulation into the wall and then hammered into place. Typical insulation materials: polystyrene, mineral fibre board, wood fibre board. Other valid steps are acceptable.

rows.verbatim: Adding an external system of insulation to the wall – Sketches
rows.contextNote: Quality of sketches for the external-insulation steps: excellent 8, good 6, fair 4. The scheme sketch shows the wall, adhesive, insulation board and mechanical fixing.

questionText: Discuss two advantages of insulating the external walls of the house.

questionText: Using a single-line labelled diagram, show the pipework required to provide hot and cold water to a mixer-shower and to provide cold water to a toilet, as shown in the sketch. Include the following on your diagram: rising main and water storage tank; hot water cylinder; typical pipework to mixer-shower and toilet; all necessary valves. On your diagram, show the insulation to the water storage tank in the attic and to all the pipework.

Marked details: rising main (typically 15 mm with stop valve); cold water storage tank; overflow (22 mm minimum); cold supply from the storage tank to the hot water cylinder (22 mm); hot water cylinder (pre-insulated); expansion pipe from the cylinder (22 mm); hot water supply to the mixer-shower (22 mm); cold water supply to the mixer-shower (22 mm); cold water supply to the toilet cistern (15 mm); valves; insulation to the storage tank and pipework; labelling. Hot and cold supplies to the shower and a cold supply to the toilet are all required.

rows.contextNote: Two distinct methods, 5 marks each for notes and sketches. Such as: a low-flow eco or aerated shower head; shorter showers and no power shower; a tap aerator, push-button or infra-red sensor taps, or an inline regulating valve on the wash hand basin; not running the tap while brushing teeth; a low-flush or dual-flush cistern, or a water-saver bag in the cistern; checking the cistern for leaks; showering rather than bathing.

rows.verbatim: pipework necessary to collect and store rainwater from the roof

stem: The sketch shows a dwelling house with a traditional slated cut roof. The roof has a pitch of 30° and is highly insulated at ceiling joist level. The internal span of the house is 5.8 metres. The walls of the house are of 450 mm rendered concrete block construction with a full-fill insulated cavity.
questionText: To a scale of 1:10, draw a vertical section through one half of the roof structure, from just below eaves up to the ridge. Show one external wall and one rafter length. Include the typical construction details from 600 mm below the ceiling joists up to the ridge, and include three courses of slate at eaves. Include four typical dimensions.

rows.contextNote: Three external-wall details, 4 each (3 for drawing, 1 for annotation). Typical: external and internal render; 100 mm external and internal block leaves; wall ties; 250 mm full-fill insulated cavity; cavity closer; 100 mm × 75 mm wallplate(s).

Four roof-structure details, 4 each (3 drawing, 1 annotation). Typical: 200 mm × 50 mm rafters at 400 mm centres; ceiling joists at 400 mm centres; 225 mm × 75 mm purlin; strut supporting the purlin; hanger; collar tie at each couple or at 1200 mm centres; ridge board; plasterboard with 350 mm insulation laid in three layers.

Four eaves details, 4 each (3 drawing, 1 annotation). Typical: tilting fillet; fascia board, soffit and gutter (any two); 25 mm fascia ventilator and 50 mm proprietary eaves ventilator; wind-tightness barrier; breather membrane laid over the rafters; 50 mm × 30 mm slating battens; three courses of slates.
Four appropriate typical dimensions on the section.
Scale 4 and drafting 4, assessed together: excellent 8, good 6, fair 4.

stem: Lifetime use of a dwelling should be a key consideration at the design stage.
questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches, discuss two best-practice guidelines that should be followed when designing for lifetime use at each of the following areas of a dwelling: entrance access.

rows.contextNote: First guideline for the entrance access: notes 4 and sketches 4. Such as: a level threshold (maximum 15 mm upstand, chamfered or rounded edges) with a recessed drainage channel and the internal floor flush; a 1000 mm minimum clear door opening; a slip-resistant approach path at 1:20 or flatter (ramps no steeper than 1:12, with level landings); a level landing of at least 1500 mm × 1500 mm outside the door and 300 mm clear space at the leading edge; a canopy or recess at least 900 mm deep; lever handles 800–1050 mm above floor level and low door-closer force; a vision panel; motion-sensor lighting.
Second, different guideline for the entrance access: notes 4 and sketches 4. Do not credit the same guideline twice.

stem: Shown in the sketch is the proposed external wall design detail for a new house of timber frame construction.
questionText: Calculate the U-value of the proposed wall, given the construction has the following sequence and data: External render thickness 16 mm External concrete block thickness 100 mm Clear cavity width 60 mm Oriented Strand Board (OSB) thickness 12 mm Timber stud thickness 250 mm Insulation between studs thickness 250 mm Oriented Strand Board (OSB) thickness 12 mm Plasterboard thickness 12.5 mm. Thermal data of the external wall: Resistance of external surface (R) 0.048 m2 ºC/W; Resistivity of external render (r) 2.170 m ºC/W; Conductivity of concrete block (k) 1.440 W/m ºC; Resistance of clear cavity (R) 0.440 m2 ºC/W; Conductivity of OSB (k) 0.130 W/m ºC; Conductivity of insulation (k) 0.039 W/m ºC; Conductivity of OSB (k) 0.130 W/m ºC; Conductivity of plasterboard (k) 0.250 W/m ºC; Resistance of internal surface (R) 0.130 m2 ºC/W. Note: The timber studs need not be considered in your calculations.

rows.contextNote: Set out the layers, thicknesses (in metres), k or r values and resistances in a table.
External surface resistance 0.048 and internal surface resistance 0.130 m²°C/W, 3 each.

Seven layer resistances, 3 each: render 0.016 × 2.170 = 0.035; concrete block 0.100 ÷ 1.440 = 0.069; clear cavity 0.440 (given); OSB 0.012 ÷ 0.130 = 0.092; insulation 0.250 ÷ 0.039 = 6.410; OSB 0.092; plasterboard 0.0125 ÷ 0.250 = 0.050 m²°C/W. The studs are ignored, as the question states.
Total resistance Rt = 7.367 m²°C/W (sum of all resistances).
U = 1 ÷ Rt = 1 ÷ 7.367 = 0.136 W/m²°C, with units.

stem: Shown in the sketch is the proposed external wall design detail for a new house of timber frame construction.

rows.contextNote: Heat loss = U × area × temperature difference = 0.136 × 144 × (20 − 7) = 254.592 W (J/s).
Heating time = 60 × 60 × 6 × 7 × 33 = 4,989,600 seconds per year.

stem: “It would be reasonable to assume that ensuring good indoor air quality would be a key factor when designing and constructing buildings. The term sick building syndrome became well known in the 1980’s and still lingers today, though largely associated with poorly air-conditioned offices. However, the health impacts of buildings are still poorly understood and rarely taken into account as a key priority when buildings are designed or renovated. Architects, when specifying building materials are mainly concerned with cost, availability, robustness and aesthetics, not their impacts on health.” Adapted from: Building Materials, Health and Indoor Air Quality: No Breathing Space by Tom Wooley
questionText: Discuss the above statement in detail.

rows.contextNote: Point 5 and discussion 5. Such as: people spend most of their lives indoors, yet health is often overlooked behind cost, appearance, durability and availability; sick building syndrome symptoms linked to poor ventilation, mould and chemical emissions.

Point 5 and discussion 5. Such as: more airtight buildings need carefully designed ventilation; VOCs and formaldehyde from paints, adhesives, finishes and composite boards; condensation and mould from poor detailing, especially in Ireland’s damp climate.

Point 5 and discussion 5. Such as: health impacts are harder to measure and appear later, while healthier materials can cost more; Passive House/EnerPHit ventilation with heat recovery, low-VOC materials, daylight and newer certification standards show a growing focus on wellbeing. Three distinct, well-argued points are needed.

stem: The external wall of a house built in the 1970s is of single leaf hollow-block construction with an external render. Insulated plasterboard is fixed to the internal surface of the wall. It is proposed to upgrade the thermal properties of the external wall by installing external insulation as shown.
questionText: Calculate the U-value of the proposed wall, given the construction has the following sequence and data: External acrylic render thickness 8 mm External polystyrene insulation thickness 100 mm External render thickness 16 mm Hollow concrete block thickness 215 mm Insulation thickness 25 mm Plasterboard thickness 12.5 mm Internal skim coat thickness 3 mm. Thermal data of the external wall: Resistance of external surface (R) 0.048 m2 ºC/W; Conductivity of acrylic render (k) 0.670 W/m ºC; Conductivity of external insulation (k) 0.030 W/m ºC; Resistivity of external render (r) 2.170 m ºC/W; Resistance of hollow concrete block (R) 0.210 m2 ºC/W; Conductivity of insulation (k) 0.037 W/m ºC; Conductivity of plasterboard (k) 0.160 W/m ºC; Resistivity of skim coat (r) 5.550 m ºC/W; Resistance of internal surface (R) 0.122 m2 ºC/W.

rows.contextNote: External surface resistance 0.048 m²°C/W (given).
Internal surface resistance 0.122 m²°C/W (given).

Seven layer resistances, 3 each: acrylic render 0.008 ÷ 0.670 = 0.012; external insulation 0.100 ÷ 0.030 = 3.333; sand cement render 0.016 × 2.170 = 0.035; hollow concrete block 0.210 (given); insulation 0.025 ÷ 0.037 = 0.676; plasterboard 0.0125 ÷ 0.160 = 0.078; internal skim coat 0.003 × 5.550 = 0.017 m²°C/W.
Total resistance Rt = 4.531 m²°C/W (sum of all resistances).
U = 1 ÷ Rt = 1 ÷ 4.531 = 0.221 W/m²°C, with units.

sourceMaterial.presentationNote: All printed data are retained in the original question. Parts (b) and (c) use the U-value from part (a); the scheme’s worked answers are U = 0.221 W/m²°C, an annual cost of €76.34 and 137 mm of additional insulation.

stem: The external wall of a house built in the 1970s is of single leaf hollow-block construction with an external render. Insulated plasterboard is fixed to the internal surface of the wall. It is proposed to upgrade the thermal properties of the external wall by installing external insulation as shown.
questionText: Using the U-value of the wall obtained at 5(a) above and the following data, calculate the cost of heat lost annually through this wall: area of external wall 144 m2; average internal temperature 19 ºC; average external temperature 6 ºC; heating period 7 hours daily for 33 weeks per annum; cost of wood pellets 55 cent per kg; calorific value of wood pellets 17350 kJ per kg; 1000 Watts 1 kJ per second.

rows.contextNote: Heat loss = U × area × temperature difference = 0.221 × 144 × (19 − 6) = 413.712 W (J/s).
Heating time = 60 × 60 × 7 × 7 × 33 = 5,821,200 seconds per year (1,344 hours).

rows.verbatim: Kgs of wood pellets for one year
rows.contextNote: Wood pellets = 2,408,300.29 ÷ 17,350 = 138.810 kg per year.
Cost = 138.810 × €0.55 = €76.34 per year. The single-formula method (U × area × ΔT × seconds × cost ÷ (calorific value × 1000)) gives the same €76.34.

questionText:

Thermal data of the external wall: Resistance of external surface (R) 0.048 m2 ºC/W; Conductivity of acrylic render (k) 0.670 W/m ºC; Conductivity of external insulation (k) 0.030 W/m ºC; Resistivity of external render (r) 2.170 m ºC/W; Resistance of hollow concrete block (R) 0.210 m2 ºC/W; Conductivity of insulation (k) 0.037 W/m ºC; Conductivity of plasterboard (k) 0.160 W/m ºC; Resistivity of skim coat (r) 5.550 m ºC/W; Resistance of internal surface (R) 0.122 m2 ºC/W.

(c) It has been decided that the wall at 5(a) above should meet the Passive House standard, by further increasing the thickness of the external insulation. Calculate the thickness of additional external insulation required to achieve a U-value of 0.11 W/m2 ºC.

rows.contextNote: External surface resistance 0.048 m²°C/W (given).
Internal surface resistance 0.122 m²°C/W (given).

Seven layer resistances, 3 each: acrylic render 0.008 ÷ 0.670 = 0.012; external insulation 0.100 ÷ 0.030 = 3.333; sand cement render 0.016 × 2.170 = 0.035; hollow concrete block 0.210 (given); insulation 0.025 ÷ 0.037 = 0.676; plasterboard 0.0125 ÷ 0.160 = 0.078; internal skim coat 0.003 × 5.550 = 0.017 m²°C/W.
Total resistance Rt = 4.531 m²°C/W (sum of all resistances).
U = 1 ÷ Rt = 1 ÷ 4.531 = 0.221 W/m²°C, with units.
Heat loss = U × area × temperature difference = 0.221 × 144 × (19 − 6) = 413.712 W (J/s).
Heating time = 60 × 60 × 7 × 7 × 33 = 5,821,200 seconds per year (1,344 hours).

rows.verbatim: Kgs of wood pellets for one year
rows.contextNote: Wood pellets = 2,408,300.29 ÷ 17,350 = 138.810 kg per year.
Cost = 138.810 × €0.55 = €76.34 per year. The single-formula method (U × area × ΔT × seconds × cost ÷ (calorific value × 1000)) gives the same €76.34.

rows.verbatim: Resistance for U-value for 0.11 W/m2 °C (using R=1/U)
rows.contextNote: Required resistance = 1 ÷ 0.11 = 9.091 m²K/W (the scheme first finds R = 1 ÷ 0.221 = 4.525 for the wall at 5(a)).
Additional resistance = 9.091 − 4.525 = 4.566 m²K/W.
R = T ÷ k for the external insulation: 4.566 = T ÷ 0.030.
T = 4.566 × 0.030 = 0.137 m, so 137 mm of additional insulation. Alternative calculation methods are acceptable.

questionText: Explain, with the aid of notes and freehand sketches, any five of the following: raft foundation; housing joint; rainwater butt; stud wall; laser level; damp-proof course; door threshold; baluster; room thermostat.

rows.contextNote: Explain any five of the nine terms. Each term is marked separately: primary communication of relevant information 6 and other communication 4, in notes or sketches (the scheme reserves no fixed split between them). Raft foundation: a large, continuous reinforced concrete slab supporting the whole structure, "floating" like a raft; spreads the load over the whole footprint, reducing pressure on the soil; suits soils of low bearing capacity; needs more steel and concrete than a strip foundation. Housing joint: a groove or slot cut across the width of one piece receives the end of another; a medium gluing area; used for shelves, cabinets and bookcases; a through housing runs fully across and shows at both ends, a stopped housing hides the joint at the front edge. Rainwater butt: a container that collects and stores rainwater from the roof via gutters and downpipes; reuses water for plants, lawns or washing the car; reduces reliance on treated tap water and lowers metered water use. Stud wall: an internal wall framed with vertical timber or metal studs covered with plasterboard on both sides; lighter and faster to build than a block wall; load-bearing or non-load-bearing; houses electrical and plumbing services; poorer sound insulation and bearing capacity than a block wall. Laser level: a tool projecting a laser beam to give a straight, level reference line, vertical and/or horizontal; a rotary laser projects a 360° beam for large or outdoor work; more accurate than a spirit level; can be mounted on tripods or clamps. Damp-proof course: a barrier stopping moisture rising through walls and floors by capillary action; polythene, bitumen felt, lead or copper, or slate; laid horizontally between courses, typically 150 mm above ground level, and around window and door openings; protects finishes and reduces mould and decay. Door threshold: the strip of wood, metal or plastic at the bottom of a doorway where the door closes; bridges two floor surfaces and seals the doorway; external thresholds keep out weather and draughts; internal ones cover changes in floor level; must meet building regulations so they are not a trip hazard. Baluster: a short vertical post, often decorative, supporting the handrail of a stairs; a row of balusters is a balustrade; a safety element preventing falls, especially by children; also on balconies and terraces; wood, metal, glass or concrete. Room thermostat: controls room temperature by switching the heating on below the set point and off above it; keeps rooms comfortable efficiently; manual dial or digital models; smart thermostats connect to Wi-Fi and a smartphone.

questionText: Explain, with the aid of notes and freehand sketches, any five of the following: triple glazing; wind turbine; carbon monoxide alarm; mortise and tenon joint; butt hinge; ball valve; cordless circular saw; fascia board; smart meter.

rows.contextNote: Explain any five of the nine terms. Each term is marked separately: primary communication of relevant information 6 and other communication 4, in notes or sketches (the scheme reserves no fixed split between them). Triple glazing: three panes of glass separated by insulating gaps, often argon-filled; more energy efficient than single or double glazing; high thermal and sound insulation; typically dearer than double glazing. Wind turbine: converts the kinetic energy of wind into electricity; renewable, emission-free generation; on land or offshore, singly or in wind farms; Ireland produces a large share of its energy from wind. Carbon monoxide alarm: detects carbon monoxide, a colourless, odourless, poisonous gas from fuel-burning appliances (boilers, stoves, fires, heaters), and sounds a warning; mandatory when installing new or replacement fossil-fuel appliances; test it regularly. Mortise and tenon joint: a tenon cut on the end of one piece fits a mortise cut in the other; very strong with a large gluing area; used for chair and table legs and rails, doors and windows; a stopped joint hides the tenon. Butt hinge: a common hinge joining a door to its frame; two rectangular leaves joined by knuckles and a pin; the leaves sit flush when the door closes; for interior or exterior doors, cabinets and lids; strong and affordable. Ball valve: controls flow with a rotating ball with a hole through it; open when the hole lines up with the pipe, closed when it is at right angles; the handle shows open, closed or partly open; used to isolate plumbing for maintenance or emergencies. Cordless circular saw: a portable battery-powered (usually lithium-ion) saw for cutting wood, and sometimes metal or plastic, without a mains cable; can make rip, cross and bevel cuts. Fascia board: a horizontal board fixed to the ends of the rafters along the lower edge of the roof; timber or uPVC; protects the rafter ends and supports the gutter; closes the roof against moisture and pests; available in colours and decorative profiles. Smart meter: an electricity meter that records use automatically and sends readings to the supplier, ending manual and estimated readings; splits use into day, night and peak times; shows usage patterns to help choose a tariff and save energy.

questionText: Explain, with the aid of notes and freehand sketches, any five of the following: box dovetail joint; triple glazing; solar panel; cordless drill; skirting board; compression fitting; natural seasoning; concrete lintel; radon barrier.

rows.contextNote: Explain any five of the nine terms. Each term is marked separately: primary communication of relevant information 6 and other communication 4, in notes or sketches (the scheme reserves no fixed split between them). Box dovetail joint: a joint for box shapes and a common joint in high-quality furniture, made by hand or with special jigs; the slope of the dovetails matters for strength, usually 1:6 in softwood and 1:8 in hardwood; it gives a decorative appearance, sometimes highlighted with contrasting woods. A sketch should show the interlocking tails and pins at the corner. Triple glazing: three panes of glass with a cavity between each; a better insulator and better acoustic performance than double glazing; low-e coatings reflect heat back into the house; cavities filled with argon or krypton reduce heat loss; an improved window U-value, a more comfortable indoor temperature and reduced condensation. A sketch should show the three panes, spacers and cavities. Solar panel: a solar collector absorbs solar radiation and converts it to heat, usually on a south-facing roof or secure ground-level fixing, working with other forms of heating and reducing CO2 emissions; types include flat-plate and evacuated-tube collectors, and tubes can be mounted to follow the sun. The scheme also lists photovoltaic panels: a coherent explanation of either is acceptable, but a photovoltaic panel produces electricity, not heat. Cordless drill: battery operated with rechargeable batteries, so not directly connected to AC mains power in use; features similar to a mains drill, including hammer action; used for driving screws, with a clutch to prevent damage to screw heads; right-angle versions for tight spaces; several power and speed settings, light low-voltage drills for DIY and heavier higher-voltage drills for robust work. A sketch should show the drill body, chuck and battery. Skirting board: a decorative board fitted at the junction of a wall and floor, giving a neat finish; hardwood, softwood or MDF in various lengths and profiles; typical sections from 100 mm × 15 mm to 200 mm × 20 mm; mitred at internal and external corners. A sketch should show the board fixed at the wall–floor junction. Compression fitting: a plumbing joint for copper or PVC pipes, made of brass or PVC in a range of sizes; the pipe ends are cut square, the nut and olive are fitted over the pipe, the pipe is pushed into the fitting and the nut is tightened to compress the olive into a watertight joint; PTFE tape may be used. A sketch should show the body, nut, olive and pipe. Natural seasoning: a traditional method of reducing the moisture content of timber; planks are stacked parallel with spaces between, separated by stickers (usually about 25 mm × 15 mm), in an open shed on a clean, dry, level base such as brick piers, and dried by the prevailing weather; plank ends are painted to prevent splitting; one species per stack; moisture content falls to about 18–22%, in equilibrium with the surrounding air; cheap because it uses no electrical energy, but slow and the rate cannot be controlled. A sketch should show the stacked planks, stickers and cover. Concrete lintel: a reinforced concrete beam spanning a door or window opening, carrying the blockwork or brickwork above and transferring the load to the wall at either side; cast in situ or, more commonly, pre-stressed; the length depends on the opening width and the imposed loads, and pre-stressed lintels come in a range of lengths and widths. A sketch should show the lintel bearing on the wall either side of the opening. Radon barrier: a flexible membrane placed under the floor and extended through the external walls to prevent radon gas entering the building; fitted over the whole floor area as one complete, unbroken layer with all joints taped and sealed, including around service pipes; usually laid over sand blinding (which protects it) and beneath the insulation; it replaces the damp proof membrane; installed with care by trained personnel so it is not damaged. Only a membrane rated and detailed as a radon barrier does this job.

stem: The sketch shows a railway keepers cottage built over 130 years ago. These traditional cottages can be seen at railway crossing points throughout our rural landscape. They form an important part of our built heritage.
questionText: A survey of the cottage reveals: 500 mm solid external wall of stone construction, uninsulated, with an internal lime render; uninsulated traditional cut roof with natural slate; single-glazed, softwood sliding sash windows. Select any two of the above areas and, using notes and freehand sketches, describe in detail the steps involved in upgrading the thermal performance of each area selected in a manner that respects the original character of the cottage.

rows.verbatim: Steps involved in upgrading the thermal performance of each area selected
rows.contextNote: Any two of the three areas, each notes 8 and sketches 12 = 20, respecting the cottage’s character. Stone wall: keep the wall breathable, with layers more vapour-permeable towards the outside and no impermeable vapour barriers; use hygroscopic natural insulation (hemp/hempcrete, lime, wood fibre, cork, sheep’s wool); rake out and repoint with lime mortar by hand (joints raked to twice their width, dampened first, filled in stages, protected with hessian while it carbonates); apply hempcrete internally and allow 4–6 weeks to dry, then lime render, or a three-coat lime plaster (scud coat, haired scratch coat, float coat, lime-putty finish). Cut roof: remove and set aside the slates, cleaning only their undersides; check and repair decayed rafters, wallplate and fascia in the same species and profile with traditional joints; treat new timber (boron); fit a vapour-permeable breathable membrane with counter-battens for ventilation; insulate with hygroscopic materials (sheep’s wool between rafters, wood fibre board above or below); keep the roof ventilated; re-lay the slates with the heaviest at the eaves, replacing broken ones with reclaimed slate; period cast-iron rainwater goods. Sash windows: repair rather than replace the original sashes, using a specialist conservation joiner; remove sashes and glass carefully, recording positions; replace only rotten timber in the same species and profiles with traditional joints and animal glue; free the pulleys, renew the sash cords and reuse the weights; reglaze with linseed-oil putty (salvaged or sourced float glass); repaint with non-toxic paint; add discreet secondary glazing to cut heat loss; record the repair.

options: Thermal upgrading of solid stone external wall
Thermal upgrading of traditional cut roof
Original sliding sash windows-softwood and single glazed

rows.verbatim: Importance when restoring traditional heritage buildings
rows.contextNote: Any two of the three principles, each discussion/notes 10. stem: A continuous thermal envelope is essential to prevent thermal bridging in a dwelling. The drawing shows a vertical section through the external leaf of a bungalow having a 450 mm concrete block wall with a 250 mm full-fill insulated cavity. The house has a truss roof and an insulated concrete ground floor. The window frame is thermally broken.
questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches, show best practice design detailing that will prevent the formation of a thermal bridge at any three locations circled on the drawing.

rows.verbatim: Best practice design detailing to prevent thermal bridging
rows.contextNote: Any three of the four circled locations, each note 8 and sketches 8 = 16, showing the continuous insulation line. Wall and roof junction: wall and roof insulation meeting to keep the envelope continuous; a thermal break at the wallplate (insulated barrier or thermal blocks); cavity insulation continued and the eaves detailed to avoid a cold bridge; no direct structural or steel connections bridging the insulation. Window Head: wall insulation continuous with the window frame insulation; thermally broken frame and insulated cavity closers at the opening; insulated lintels or thermal-break details above the window; airtight seals around the frame. Window cill: wall insulation and cavity closers continued around the opening; an insulated cill detail or insulation behind the concrete cill; thermally broken frame with insulated perimeter seals; airtight frame-to-wall junction. Wall and floor junction: floor and wall insulation continuous; insulated slab-edge (perimeter) detail; cavity insulation taken down to meet the floor insulation; thermal blocks where the slab abuts the external wall, with no exposed concrete bridging inside to outside.

options: Wall and roof junction
Window Head
Window cill
Wall and floor junction

questionText:
(a) Discuss in detail the importance of any two of the following in maintaining a positive health and safety culture among workers on a construction site: safety training; health and safety officer; risk assessment audit.

(b) Outline one possible risk to personal safety associated with each of the following: working in a deep trench; installing insulation in an attic space; repairing a chimney capping.

(c) For each risk discussed at 2(b) above, show, using notes and freehand sketches, two best practice guidelines that should be observed to reduce the possibility of injury to a worker undertaking each task.

rows.verbatim: The importance of any two in maintaining a positive health and safety culture
rows.contextNote: Any two of the three, 6 each, discussing why each matters to a positive health and safety culture. Safety training: Safe Pass is mandatory and kept current through refresher courses; training builds awareness of site risks and the skills to identify them and follow best practice; specialist tickets for machinery and vehicles; monitoring and enforcing safe work practices; it may be a condition of the insurance provider. Health and safety officer: provides induction and ongoing training (working at heights, machinery use); develops emergency response plans; keeps first aid and emergency equipment available; ensures the correct PPE is worn; carries out safety inspections and risk assessments; reviews the safety statement; investigates, records and reports accidents. Risk assessment audit: provides a safe working environment; evaluates compliance with safety regulations and policies; identifies hazards and puts control measures in place where a risk cannot be eliminated (for fire: alarms, evacuation signage, drills, extinguishers); recommends improvements; identifies training needs; reduces accidents and liability.

options: Safety training
Health and safety officer
Risk assessment audit

rows.contextNote: One risk outlined. Such as: workers seriously injured or buried if the trench sides collapse; machinery or vehicles falling in; materials stored too close to the edge causing a collapse; falling into an unguarded trench; materials falling in; nearby structures undermined.

rows.contextNote: One risk outlined. Such as: falling through the plasterboard ceiling; injury when cutting the insulation; skin or eye irritation without a coverall, gloves and goggles; electrocution from exposed wires; fire if insulation covers recessed lights; lung damage from inhaled machine-made mineral fibres (MMMFs).

stem: An airtight external building envelope is important in the design of a dwelling house.
questionText: The drawing shows an outline section of a two-storey house having a 450 mm external concrete block wall with a 250 mm full-fill insulated cavity. The house has a truss roof and a first floor of timber construction. The external door has a thermally broken frame. A Mechanical Ventilation with Heat Recovery system supplies ventilation through ceiling ducts. Using notes and freehand sketches, show best practice design detailing that will prevent air leakage at any three of the locations circled on the drawing.

rows.verbatim: Best practice design detailing to prevent air leakage at any three of the locations circled
rows.contextNote: Any three of the four circled locations, each notes 8 and sketches 8 = 16, showing the continuous airtight layer. Head of external door: seal the thermally broken door frame to the reveal of the inner block wall with plasterable airtightness tape, then plaster over the tape; or airtightness paint on the reveal before plastering, or slabbing and skimming. First floor junction with external wall: make the wall airtight where the joists bear — an airtightness membrane sealed with airtight silicone or plasterable tape, or sand cement render or airtightness paint; tape each joist where it breaks the airtightness barrier; seal the floor/wall and roof/wall junctions with tape or paint. Wallplate level: an airtightness membrane under the ceiling joists, wrapped onto the wallplate and down onto the first block below it, fixed to the wall with plasterable airtightness tape or a bead of airtight silicone, then scrim or mesh and sand cement plaster. MVHR duct protruding through the ceiling: an airtightness membrane under the joists, sealed to the duct with a self-adhesive grommet fixed to the membrane, or by carefully taping the duct to the membrane with airtightness tape.

options: Head of external door
First floor junction with external wall

stem: The sketch shows the proposed design of a Passive House which is to be constructed in a rural setting.
questionText:
(a) Using notes and freehand sketches, discuss the importance of any two of the following in Passive House design: building form; foundation design; space heating energy demand.

(b) Using notes and freehand sketches, suggest a preferred orientation for the house shown. Show the sun path on your sketch. Discuss two benefits to the homeowner of your preferred orientation.

(c) Solar overheating may occur during the summer months in the house shown. Using notes and freehand sketches, suggest two ways to reduce the possibility of solar overheating while respecting the character of this house design.

rows.verbatim: Discuss the importance of any two in Passive House design
rows.contextNote: Any two of the three, each notes 5 and sketches 5 = 10. Building form: a compact, simple rectangular form with the smallest surface area (A/V ratio 0.7 or less) to cut heat loss, materials and cost; a narrow plan, one room deep, to maximise solar gain; clean lines in walls and roof that make airtightness easy. Foundation design: insulated ring-beam or passive raft foundations wrapped in insulation to eliminate thermal bridging; thermal blocks in the inner-leaf rising wall; 50–100 mm edge insulation at the floor/wall junction; thermally broken wall ties; a U-value of 0.10–0.15 W/m²K. Space heating energy demand: passive house space-heating demand of no more than 15 kWh/m² per year; quality workmanship in airtightness and insulation; eliminating thermal bridges; solar gain through well-designed fenestration; solar shading, thermal mass and controlled ventilation to keep about 20 °C all year.

Foundation design
Space heating energy demand

questionText: Discuss the importance of any two of the following in the eco-refurbishment of an old house built in the vernacular tradition: respect for local character; breathable structure; reuse of materials.

rows.contextNote: Any two of the three, 10 each, as a developed discussion; the scheme does not split the 10 into points. Respect for local character: vernacular houses evolved from their location, built simply and modestly from local materials and labour, so refurbishment keeps materials, methods and detailing simple, retains the historic character and the unity of the row of cottages, upgrades the fabric first, and takes advice from a conservation officer, architect, engineer or designer. Breathable structure: moisture moves gradually from the inside through the walls and roof and is not trapped, preventing surface and interstitial condensation; natural, hygroscopic insulation and finishes (lime, hemp, cork, wood fibreboard, sheep’s wool, lime renders and plasters) let it move; vapour barriers and vapour-resistant materials are not usually appropriate in older buildings, and layers should become more permeable from inside to outside. questionText: A row of single-storey cottages is shown in the sketch. One of the cottages is in need of significant refurbishment. A survey of the cottage reveals: un-insulated traditional cut roof with natural slates; softwood windows, single-glazed with sliding sash; un-insulated suspended timber floor. Select any two of the areas at 4(b) above and, using notes and freehand sketches, describe the steps involved in upgrading each area selected in a manner that respects the appearance and character of the original cottages.

rows.verbatim: Two areas for upgrading - roof, windows, floor
rows.contextNote: Any two of the three surveyed areas, each notes 10 and sketches 10 = 20, describing the upgrading steps in a way that respects the appearance and character of the original cottages. Roof: retain as much historic fabric as possible; remove, number and store the slates and reuse them (slates from the rear placed on the front for uniformity); inspect the members and replace only decayed portions; replace impermeable sarking felt with a vapour-diffuse membrane; insulate with hygroscopic materials (sheep’s wool between the rafters, wood fibreboard above and below) with counter battens for ventilation, or, as the scheme’s other option, insulation with a ventilation path and a continuous taped vapour barrier on the warm side behind an insulated service cavity. Sliding sash windows: maintain and repair before replacing; survey, number and remove the sashes; repair damaged wood with a similar species, sand, seal and repaint; remove cracked putty and re-glaze with linseed oil putty; check the pulleys and cords; then keep the existing glass, or fit draught-proof seals and double-glazed units where the rebates are deep enough, or fit secondary glazing inside. Suspended timber floor: determine the floor’s historical significance; record and number the floorboards and skirting, remove and store them; check the sub-floor ventilation; replace decayed joists or boards; fit insulation between the joists on netting or battens, friction tight with no gaps; fit a breather membrane and replace the floorboards as labelled.

options: Roof
Sliding sash windows
Suspended timber floor

questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches, discuss the importance of any two of the following in designing a house to have low environmental impact: compact form; flexible design; low maintenance.

rows.contextNote: Any two of the three, each notes 5 and sketches 5 = 10. Compact form: a reduced external surface area minimises heat loss and the materials needed to enclose the living space; less concrete and so lower carbon emissions; a smaller heated air volume; a house one room wide is easier to heat by passive solar gain; less land used and less visual impact. Flexible design: the dwelling can respond over time to changes in lifestyle and needs without major structural change, extending its useful life; a bathroom designed for lifetime use; a home office or occasional bedroom easily made; a wall to the hallway removable to form a larger open-plan area; easier retrofitting of new technologies. Low maintenance: reduces the energy and materials used over the dwelling’s lifetime and delays its replacement; keeps the energy-saving features at peak efficiency for longer; robust construction; keeps the attractive, unobtrusive appearance for longer.

options: Compact form
Flexible design
Low maintenance

stem: It is proposed to design the external envelope of a dwelling house to be thermal bridge free. The drawing shows an outline section through a two-storey house having a 450 mm external concrete block wall with a 250 mm full-fill insulated cavity. The roof is a traditional cut roof, the first floor has tongue-and-groove flooring on timber joists and the ground floor is an insulated solid concrete floor.
questionText: Select any three locations from those circled on the drawing and, using notes and freehand sketches, show best practice design detailing that will prevent the formation of a thermal bridge at each location selected.

rows.contextNote: Any three of the four circled locations, each notes 8 and sketches 8 = 16, showing the insulation kept continuous so that no thermal bridge forms. Junction of roof and wall at eaves: 60 mm rigid insulation board; 400 mm fibreglass insulation; a 60 mm cavity closer; an autoclaved aerated concrete (AAC) block; 250 mm full-fill cavity insulation. Junction of upper floors and external walls: joists hung on the inside leaf, on metal hangers or resin-anchored bolts, with no penetration of the leaf and cavity; the wall plastered for airtightness. Window cill: insulation at the back of the cill so it does not bridge the cavity; a high-density proprietary cavity closer; 250 mm full-fill cavity insulation; airtightness tape to the triple-glazed window frame. Ground floors abutting external walls: cavity insulation carried down at least 225 mm below the top of the finished floor; an 80 mm perimeter insulation strip between the slab and the inner leaf; 150–300 mm insulation under the slab; 100 mm AAC blocks below ground level.

questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches, discuss in detail the importance of any two of the following in the design of a Passive House: airtight building envelope; space heating demand; indoor air quality.

rows.verbatim: Design of a Passive House - any 2
rows.contextNote: Any two of the three, each notes 8 and sketches 8 = 16. Airtight building envelope: build tight and ventilate right; an unbroken air barrier on the warm side of the insulation, taped at every junction (wall/floor, wall/window, wall/door, ceiling/wall, chimney/ceiling), prevents unregulated air leakage and heat loss and lets the fresh-air intake be controlled; a service cavity keeps services from puncturing it; grommets seal pipes and cables; a blower door test checks it. Space heating demand: the energy needed to keep 20 °C indoors all year, not including hot water; a Passive House limits it to 15 kWh/m² per year or less, with a heating load of no more than 10 W/m²; the 2015 scheme also cites a primary energy demand of no more than 120 kWh/m² per year. Indoor air quality: greater airtightness needs a designed ventilation system that supplies clean, warm, filtered fresh air; mechanical ventilation with heat recovery extracts moist air from the kitchen, utility and bathrooms and passes it through a heat exchanger without mixing it with the incoming air; filters changed every three to six months; relative humidity of 30% to 60%; 0.3 to 0.6 air changes per hour.

options: Airtight building envelope
Space heating demand
Indoor air quality

stem: The sketch shows a proposed external wall design for a new house. The external wall is constructed using Insulated Concrete Formwork (ICF).
questionText:
Calculate the U-value of the wall, given the construction has the following sequence and data: Acrylic external render thickness 12 mm; external insulation thickness 150 mm; concrete thickness 150 mm; internal insulation thickness 50 mm; internal plasterboard thickness 12.5 mm; internal skim coat thickness 4 mm.
Thermal data of the external wall: resistance of external surface (R) 0.048 m² °C/W; conductivity of acrylic external render (k) 0.670 W/m °C; conductivity of external insulation (k) 0.030 W/m °C; conductivity of concrete (k) 1.280 W/m °C; conductivity of internal insulation (k) 0.030 W/m °C; conductivity of plasterboard (k) 0.250 W/m °C; resistivity of skim coat (r) 5.550 m °C/W; resistance of internal surface (R) 0.122 m² °C/W.

rows.contextNote: A clear table of the materials with their conductivity or resistivity, thickness in metres and resistance.

Eight resistances, 3 each, by R = T/k (or R = T × r for the skim coat): external surface 0.048 (given); acrylic render 0.012/0.670 = 0.018; external insulation 0.150/0.030 = 5.000; concrete 0.150/1.280 = 0.117; internal insulation 0.050/0.030 = 1.667; plasterboard 0.0125/0.250 = 0.050; skim coat 0.004 × 5.550 = 0.022; internal surface 0.122 (given). All in m²°C/W.
Total resistance Rt = 7.044 m²°C/W (the sum of all the resistances).
U = 1 ÷ Rt = 1 ÷ 7.044 = 0.142 W/m²°C, with units.

stem: The sketch shows a proposed external wall design for a new house. The external wall is constructed using Insulated Concrete Formwork (ICF).
questionText: Using the U-value of the wall obtained at 5(a) above and the following data, calculate the cost of heat lost annually through this wall: area of external wall 110 m²; average internal temperature 20 °C; average external temperature 6 °C; heating period 6 hours daily for 32 weeks per annum; cost of wood pellets 52 cent per kg; calorific value of wood pellets 17350 kJ per kg; 1000 watts: 1 kJ per second.

rows.contextNote: Heat loss = U-value × area × temperature difference = 0.142 × 110 × (20 − 6) = 218.6269 watts (joules per second).
Heating period = 60 × 60 × 7 × 6 × 32 = 4,838,400 seconds (1,344 hours).

rows.verbatim: Kgs of wood pellets for one year
rows.contextNote: Wood pellets = 1,057,804 ÷ 17,350 = 60.96 kg per year.
Annual cost = 60.96 × €0.52 = €31.71. The scheme’s alternative one-line method gives the same €31.71.

stem: The elevation and ground floor plan of a house constructed in an urban area are shown. The external walls are of timber frame construction with a rendered concrete block and brick finish. Space heating is provided using a renewable heat source. The house was designed to be energy-efficient and to have a low environmental impact.
questionText:
(a) Discuss using notes and freehand sketches, three features of the design that contribute to the house having a low environmental impact.

(b) Discuss using notes and freehand sketches, two features that could be added to the house that would further increase the energy efficiency of the house.

(c) Discuss two advantages of designing energy efficient new homes.

rows.contextNote: Notes 5 and sketches 5. Such as: timber frame from local sources — less transport, lower embodied energy than block, and carbon stored in the timber.

A second, different feature: notes 5 and sketches 5. Such as: large south-facing glazed openings filling the living spaces with light and solar heat; high-performance glazing (U-value at least 0.8 W/m²K).

A third, different feature: notes 5 and sketches 5. Such as: high insulation levels in floor, walls and roof; a one-room-deep plan lit from three sides; no chimney, so fewer draughts and better airtightness.

stem: The sketch shows a wood burning stove used to provide hot water and central heating for a two-storey house.

(c) Underfloor heating is often installed in dwellings to provide space heating. Discuss two advantages and two disadvantages of incorporating an underfloor heating system into a dwelling house.

stem: The sketch shows a bungalow which has been retrofitted. The owners have engaged skilled labour in the upgrade of their bungalow to meet the EnerPHit Passive House design standard.
questionText:
(a) Using notes and freehand sketches, discuss the importance of any two of the following when carrying out a retrofit to achieve the EnerPHit Passive House design standard: airtightness; windows; building fabric.

(b) Using notes and freehand sketches, discuss in detail how each of the following could be improved, when upgrading an existing building to meet the EnerPHit standard: indoor air quality; space heating.

(c) Discuss two advantages of using qualified skilled labour when retrofitting a house to meet EnerPHit Passive House standards.

rows.verbatim: Discuss the importance of any two in EnerPHit design standard
rows.contextNote: Any two of the three, each notes 6 and sketches 6 = 12. EnerPHit is reached through the five Passive House principles (insulation, limited thermal bridging, triple glazing, airtightness, MVHR), modelled in the PHPP design tool; its space heating demand limit is 25 kWh/m² per year (Passive House 15). Airtightness: Air leakage prevented with airtightness membranes, airtight boards and tapes in timber frame and roofs, and a sand-cement scratch coat, plaster and airtightness paint in block walls; checks for leakage at each stage and a full airtightness test at the end; the EnerPHit target is under 1.0 air changes per hour at 50 Pascals (Passive House 0.6); without airtightness the insulation cannot perform. Windows: Passive House triple-glazed windows of 0.80 W/m²K or less (EnerPHit, installed, 0.85 W/m²K or less); frames in line with the external insulation to avoid a thermal bridge; shading and ventilation planned against summer overheating. Building fabric: Insulation increased to roof, floor and walls (U-value 0.120 W/m²K or less for EnerPHit) by cavity, external or internal insulation; quality workmanship to avoid thermal bridges; external insulation continued below ground level; airtightness and insulation achieved together.

options: Airtightness
Windows
Building fabric

rows.contextNote: Such as: mechanical ventilation with heat recovery (MVHR) supplying fresh air and recovering heat, with regular filter changes; low-VOC materials, finishes and furnishings; humidity kept at 30–50% with humidity-controlled ventilation; air-quality sensors; openable windows in every room.
Freehand sketches of the improvement, such as the MVHR supply and extract routes.

Such as: continuous high-quality insulation without thermal bridges; high-performance glazing and doors with sealed junctions; an air-source or ground-source heat pump (coefficient of performance about 5:1) with underfloor heating; MVHR heat recovery; passive solar gain and thermal mass, with shading against overheating, for a steady 20 °C.
Freehand sketches of the improvement.
Point 2 and discussion 4. Such as: expertise in the complex EnerPHit requirements and best practice; quality workmanship so every component is installed correctly and the energy targets are met.

A second, different advantage: point 2 and discussion 4. Such as: efficient, on-time completion; compliance with regulations, including airtightness; problem solving on site; long-term performance, so the disruptive retrofit need not be repeated.
