stem: “Buildings have an impact on the environment at every stage of their lifecycle. Materials have to be quarried, mined or harvested, transported to factories and manufactured. The final products have to be transported to site, lifted into place and fixed in position. The buildings have to be operated, heated and cooled. Over a 60 year life cycle, components fail, roof finishes fail and need replacement, finishes spoil and need repainting and replacement. Eventually the building ceases to provide its function and needs to be deconstructed and all its components disposed by landfill, incineration, recycling or direct reuse.” Adapted from: Towards a circular economy in construction. Published by: Irish Green Building Council.
questionText: Discuss the above statement in detail.

rows.verbatim: Discussion Point 1 (4 for point, 6 for discussion)
rows.contextNote: Point 4 and discussion 6. Such as: the environmental impact of a dwelling at every stage of its lifecycle; weighing the embodied energy of materials against their operational energy — short-lived components carry a higher carbon footprint.

rows.verbatim: Discussion Point 2 (4 for point, 6 for discussion)
rows.contextNote: Point 4 and discussion 6. Such as: Environmental Product Declarations (EPD), “cradle to grave”, measuring global warming potential and other impacts, with the Irish EPD programme of the Irish Green Building Council.

rows.verbatim: Discussion Point 3 (4 for point, 6 for discussion)
rows.contextNote: Point 4 and discussion 6. Such as: the circular economy — materials kept in loops of reuse, remanufacture and recycling at their highest value, the opposite of take-make-dispose; careful design that needs less heating and cooling over the building’s life. Three distinct, well-argued points are needed.

stem: The sketch shows a site dumper in operation on a construction site.
questionText:

(b) Using notes and freehand sketches, show three items of personal protective equipment (PPE) which should be worn by workers when working with construction vehicles. Give one specific reason why each item of personal protective equipment must be worn.

rows.contextNote: Such as: wear suitable PPE (hard hat, steel-toe boots, hi-visibility clothing); inspect the vehicle before use; always wear the seatbelt; check the area for obstacles, holes or overhead power lines.

stem: An extension to a house has a highly insulated flat roof with a waterproof roof covering, as shown.
questionText:
Calculate the U-value of the roof, given the construction has the following sequence and data: Waterproof covering thickness 2 mm; roof insulation thickness 150 mm; plywood decking thickness 20 mm; clear cavity between roof joists thickness 200 mm; ceiling insulation thickness 50 mm; plasterboard thickness 12.5 mm.
Thermal data of the flat roof: resistance of external surface (R) 0.048 m² °C/W; resistivity of waterproof covering (r) 6.250 m °C/W; conductivity of roof insulation (k) 0.022 W/m °C; conductivity of plywood (k) 0.130 W/m °C; resistance of clear cavity (R) 0.170 m² °C/W; conductivity of ceiling insulation (k) 0.022 W/m °C; conductivity of plasterboard (k) 0.250 W/m °C; resistance of internal surface (R) 0.122 m² °C/W.

rows.contextNote: Eight resistances, 3 each, by R = T/k (or R = T × r): external surface 0.048 (given); waterproof covering 0.002 × 6.250 = 0.013; roof insulation 0.150/0.022 = 6.818; plywood 0.020/0.130 = 0.154; clear cavity 0.170 (given); ceiling insulation 0.050/0.022 = 2.273; plasterboard 0.0125/0.250 = 0.050; internal surface 0.122 (given). All in m²°C/W.
Total resistance Rt = 9.647 m²°C/W (the sum of all the resistances).
U = 1 ÷ Rt = 1 ÷ 9.647 = 0.104 W/m²°C, with units.

stem: An extension to a house has a highly insulated flat roof with a waterproof roof covering, as shown.
questionText:
(a) Calculate the U-value of the roof, given the construction has the following sequence and data: Waterproof covering thickness 2 mm; roof insulation thickness 150 mm; plywood decking thickness 20 mm; clear cavity between roof joists thickness 200 mm; ceiling insulation thickness 50 mm; plasterboard thickness 12.5 mm.
Thermal data of the flat roof: resistance of external surface (R) 0.048 m² °C/W; resistivity of waterproof covering (r) 6.250 m °C/W; conductivity of roof insulation (k) 0.022 W/m °C; conductivity of plywood (k) 0.130 W/m °C; resistance of clear cavity (R) 0.170 m² °C/W; conductivity of ceiling insulation (k) 0.022 W/m °C; conductivity of plasterboard (k) 0.250 W/m °C; resistance of internal surface (R) 0.122 m² °C/W.

(b) Using the U-value of the roof obtained at 5(a) above and the following data, calculate the cost of heat lost annually through this roof: dimensions of flat roof 8.5 metres × 4.5 metres; average internal temperature 18 °C; average external temperature 5 °C; heating period 8 hours daily for 36 weeks per annum; cost of oil €1.25 per litre; calorific value of oil 37350 kJ per litre; 1000 watts: 1 kJ per second.

(c) Using notes and a freehand sketch, show best practice design detailing that will prevent the formation of a thermal bridge at the abutment of the flat roof and external concrete block wall with a full-fill insulated cavity.

rows.contextNote: Eight resistances, 3 each, by R = T/k (or R = T × r): external surface 0.048 (given); waterproof covering 0.002 × 6.250 = 0.013; roof insulation 0.150/0.022 = 6.818; plywood 0.020/0.130 = 0.154; clear cavity 0.170 (given); ceiling insulation 0.050/0.022 = 2.273; plasterboard 0.0125/0.250 = 0.050; internal surface 0.122 (given). All in m²°C/W.
Total resistance Rt = 9.647 m²°C/W (the sum of all the resistances).
U = 1 ÷ Rt = 1 ÷ 9.647 = 0.104 W/m²°C, with units.
Heat loss = U-value × area × temperature difference = 0.104 × 38.25 × (18 − 5) = 51.714 watts (joules per second).

rows.verbatim: Heating duration - calculation for one year
rows.contextNote: Heating period = 60 × 60 × 7 × 8 × 36 = 7,257,600 seconds (2,016 hours).

rows.verbatim: Litres of oil - calculation for one year
rows.contextNote: Oil = 375,319 ÷ 37,350 = 10.04 litres per year.

rows.verbatim: Annual cost – calculation of heat loss PA
rows.contextNote: Annual cost = 10.04 × €1.25 = €12.53. The scheme’s alternative one-line method gives the same €12.53.

questionText:

rows.verbatim: Discuss two Passive House design features
rows.contextNote: Any two of the three, each notes 5 and sketches 5 = 10. Foundation design: highly insulated to a U-value of 0.10–0.15 W/m²K; no thermal bridge at the wall-floor junction; aerated concrete blocks at critical junctions; insulation with high compressive strength; an insulated Passive raft-type foundation. Solar shading: prevents overheating by admitting low winter sun and blocking high summer sun; overhangs or deeper eaves; fixed or adjustable brise-soleil, external blinds, awnings and sliding screens; trees and climbing plants. Thermally efficient building envelope: an unbroken line of insulation and airtightness around the whole building, with every element at its optimum performance; a constant, predictable internal temperature; lower energy use, costs and carbon.

stem: “People regardless of age, size, ability or disability are positively contributing to the social, economic and cultural life of our communities. However, finding suitable and appropriate homes that can accommodate our changing needs over time can be difficult - whether for families with young children, a person with a temporary or permanent injury, someone with a disability, or an older person living independently. Universal Design can meet everyone’s needs through flexible homes designed to adapt to lifecycle and lifestyle patterns of people over time.” Adapted from: Universal Design Guidelines for Homes in Ireland Published by National Disability Authority
questionText: Discuss the above statement in detail.

rows.contextNote: Point 4 and discussion 6. Such as: an ageing population, with those over 65 set to more than double by 2050; a 60% chance a new home will be occupied by someone with a disability; most people prefer to age in place.

rows.contextNote: Point 4 and discussion 6. Such as: Universal Design is good design — flexible, easily adapted, cost and energy effective, working as well for a newborn as for a grandparent. Three distinct, well-argued points are needed.

stem: The proposed external wall design detail for a new house is a 215 mm single leaf wall of solid block construction with external insulation, as shown.
questionText:
Calculate the U-value of the wall, given the construction has the following sequence and data: Acrylic external render thickness 8 mm; external insulation thickness 150 mm; external scratch coat thickness 10 mm; concrete block thickness 215 mm; internal plaster thickness 12 mm.
Thermal data of the external wall: resistance of external surface (R) 0.048 m2 ⁰C/W; conductivity of acrylic external render (k) 0.670 W/m ⁰C; conductivity of external insulation (k) 0.031 W/m ⁰C; conductivity of external scratch coat (k) 2.170 W/m ⁰C; conductivity of concrete blockwork (k) 1.440 W/m ⁰C; resistivity of internal plaster (r) 4.550 m ⁰C/W; resistance of internal surface (R) 0.122 m2 ⁰C/W.

rows.contextNote: A clear table of the materials with their conductivity or resistivity, thickness in metres and resistance.

Seven resistances, 3 each, by R = T/k (or R = T × r for the plaster): external surface 0.048 (given); acrylic render 0.008/0.670 = 0.012; external insulation 0.150/0.031 = 4.839; scratch coat 0.010/2.170 = 0.005; blockwork 0.215/1.44 = 0.149; internal plaster 0.012 × 4.550 = 0.055; internal surface 0.122 (given). All in m²°C/W.
Total resistance Rt = 5.229 m²°C/W (the sum of all the resistances).
U = 1 ÷ Rt = 1 ÷ 5.229 = 0.191 W/m²°C, with units.

stem: The proposed external wall design detail for a new house is a 215 mm single leaf wall of solid block construction with external insulation, as shown.
questionText:
(a) Calculate the U-value of the wall, given the construction has the following sequence and data: Acrylic external render thickness 8 mm; external insulation thickness 150 mm; external scratch coat thickness 10 mm; concrete block thickness 215 mm; internal plaster thickness 12 mm.
Thermal data of the external wall: resistance of external surface (R) 0.048 m2 ⁰C/W; conductivity of acrylic external render (k) 0.670 W/m ⁰C; conductivity of external insulation (k) 0.031 W/m ⁰C; conductivity of external scratch coat (k) 2.170 W/m ⁰C; conductivity of concrete blockwork (k) 1.440 W/m ⁰C; resistivity of internal plaster (r) 4.550 m ⁰C/W; resistance of internal surface (R) 0.122 m2 ⁰C/W.

(b) Using the U-value of the wall obtained at 5(a) above and the following data, calculate the cost of heat lost annually through this wall: area of external wall 144 m2; average internal temperature 20 ⁰C; average external temperature 5 ⁰C; heating period 10 hours daily for 37 weeks per annum; cost of oil 97 cent per litre; calorific value of oil 37350 kJ per litre; 1000 watts: 1 kJ per second.

(c) It is proposed to redesign the above external wall and upgrade its thermal properties to meet the Passive House standard by increasing the width of external insulation in the design. Calculate the thickness of additional external insulation required to achieve a U-value of 0.12 W/m2 ⁰C.

rows.contextNote: A clear table of the materials with their conductivity or resistivity, thickness in metres and resistance.

Seven resistances, 3 each, by R = T/k (or R = T × r for the plaster): external surface 0.048 (given); acrylic render 0.008/0.670 = 0.012; external insulation 0.150/0.031 = 4.839; scratch coat 0.010/2.170 = 0.005; blockwork 0.215/1.44 = 0.149; internal plaster 0.012 × 4.550 = 0.055; internal surface 0.122 (given). All in m²°C/W.
Total resistance Rt = 5.229 m²°C/W (the sum of all the resistances).
U = 1 ÷ Rt = 1 ÷ 5.229 = 0.191 W/m²°C, with units.
Heat loss = U-value × area × temperature difference = 0.191 × 144 × (20 − 5) = 413.068 watts (joules per second).
Heating period = 60 × 60 × 7 × 10 × 37 = 9,324,000 seconds (2,590 hours).

rows.verbatim: Litres of oil for one year

rows.contextNote: Annual cost = 103.118 × €0.97 = €100.02. The scheme’s alternative one-line method gives the same €100.02.

rows.verbatim: Resistance for U- value for 0.12 W/m2 °c (using R=1/U)
rows.contextNote: Required resistance = 1 ÷ 0.12 = 8.333 m²°C/W.

rows.verbatim: Resistance from calculated U-value from part (a)
rows.contextNote: Resistance of the wall from (a) = 1 ÷ 0.191 = 5.229 m²°C/W.
Difference = 8.333 − 5.229 = 3.104 m²°C/W.

rows.verbatim: Required thickness of insulation in mm.
rows.contextNote: Additional insulation = 96 mm (95 or 97 mm accepted). Alternative calculation methods are acceptable.

stem: An airtight external building envelope is vital in the design of a nearly Zero Energy Building (nZEB).
questionText:
(a) Discuss in detail two advantages of an airtight dwelling house.

(b) The drawing shows an outline section through a portion of a house. The house has a truss roof. The wall is of timber frame construction with an external concrete block leaf and the window frame is thermally broken. Using notes and freehand sketches, show best practice design detailing that will prevent air leakage at any two of the locations circled on the drawing.

(c) Describe using notes and freehand sketches, one test that is carried out to determine the airtightness of a house.

rows.contextNote: Point 3 and discussion 3. Such as: comfort without draughts; less heat lost through gaps in the fabric.
A second, different advantage. Such as: better indoor air quality; moisture kept out of the fabric; insulation and mechanical ventilation work better; less noise; lower carbon emissions.

rows.verbatim: Best practice design detailing to prevent air leakage
rows.contextNote: Any two of the three circled locations, each notes 9 and sketches 9 = 18. Head of window detail: an airtight membrane on the inner face of the timber frame, the thermally broken frame sealed to the frame and the junction taped with airtightness tape. Wallplate position detail: the wall membrane with a service cavity inside it, a membrane under the ceiling joists and the junction of the two taped. Light fitting detail: the ceiling membrane under the joists with the cable sealed through it by an airtightness grommet or self-adhesive patch.

options: Head of window detail
Wallplate position detail
Light fitting detail

rows.contextNote: Such as, the blower door test by a trained professional: a frame and panel in an external doorway with a variable-speed fan, pressure gauge and airflow measurement; the fan lowers (or raises) the pressure inside so air flows through every gap; leaks may be found with an infrared camera or smoke pencil; the result gives the air infiltration rate.
Freehand sketches of the test, such as the fan in the door frame.

stem: “Older gas and oil-fired boilers are wasteful of energy and costly to run because of the amount of fuel needed to maintain adequate comfort levels and hot water in the home. Replacing a conventional heating system with an air source heat pump system can transform the comfort levels in your home while reducing running costs, energy usage and harmful greenhouse gas emissions.” Adapted from: Home Upgrades. Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland Published on: www.seai.ie
questionText: Discuss the above statement in detail.

rows.verbatim: Discussion Point 1 (4 for point, 6 for discussion)
rows.contextNote: Point 4 and discussion 6. Such as: older oil and gas boilers are only 65–75% efficient (condensing boilers at best 80%) and burn fossil fuels with high CO₂ emissions.

rows.verbatim: Discussion Point 2 (4 for point, 6 for discussion)
rows.contextNote: Point 4 and discussion 6. Such as: rising fossil-fuel costs and fuel poverty; finite fuels whose search threatens pristine environments.

rows.verbatim: Discussion Point 3 (4 for point, 6 for discussion)
rows.contextNote: Point 4 and discussion 6. Such as: heat pumps cut carbon emissions by up to 70%, have a coefficient of performance of 3–4, are grant aided by SEAI and suit airtight, well-insulated houses. Three distinct, well-argued points are needed.
